framing: Every chosen token changes what the model sees next
paragraphs: The operation that chooses tokens determines repetition, lexical variety, search cost, and whether a generated reply preserves a constrained schema. It belongs in system design and automated evaluation alongside model weights.

The single highest-probability next word can begin a weak full sentence, and even the globally highest-scoring sequence may miss the user's goal. These distinctions separate local argmax, beam search, and stochastic sampling.

Trace one natural sentence prefix, "The autumn light is", through greedy decoding, beam search, temperature scaling, top-k, top-p, min-p, and repetition penalties. Small numerical examples show how transform order can empty a candidate pool that originally contained a legal token.

Compare each sampler setting directly on the serving path before shipping a configuration. Hosted APIs increasingly restrict or ignore sampling parameters, so verify which controls remain available and test alternatives through schema constraints and verification.
outcomes: Tell greedy choices, beam paths, and sampled continuations apart, and know when each one fits.
Compute how temperature and each candidate filter change a row of probabilities.
Explain how processing order, stopping rules, and seeds affect what you serve.
question: Which order of processing steps could remove every legal next token, even though the original row contained one?
